title: Security+ SY0-701
description: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 exam prep: 875 cards across the 5 exam domains and 28 objectives.

sources.packt: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide (Packt, 3rd ed.), condensed and corrected in my own words

cards.def: A security control implemented by technology (hardware, software, firmware), e.g. firewalls, encryption, EDR. Also called a logical control.
A control set by management through policies, plans, and oversight, e.g. risk assessments, performance reviews, code of conduct. Also called administrative.
A control carried out by people in day-to-day work, e.g. security awareness training, incident response procedures, user access management.
A tangible control you can touch that protects facilities and equipment, e.g. fences, locks, guards, CCTV, bollards.
Stops an incident before it happens, e.g. firewall ACL, door lock.
Discourages an attacker by creating a perceived risk, e.g. warning signs, visible cameras, login banners.
Identifies an incident during or after it occurs, e.g. SIEM alerts, audits, IDS, logs.
Fixes the problem and restores normal operations after an incident, e.g. restoring from backup, patching.
An alternative control used when the primary control isn't feasible or sufficient, e.g. isolating an unpatchable legacy system.
Tells people what to do, e.g. SOPs, code of conduct, AUP, regulatory reporting requirements.
Two-door enclosed area where the first door must close before the second opens, so one person at a time enters; stops tailgating (formerly a mantrap).
A seal that visibly breaks or changes color if someone opens the item it protects.
Category = HOW a control is implemented (technical, managerial, operational, physical). Type = WHAT it does (preventive, deterrent, detective, corrective, compensating, directive).
Confidentiality (only authorized people see data), Integrity (data isn't altered), Availability (data and systems are accessible when needed).
Keeping data hidden from unauthorized people. Tools: encryption, access controls, MFA.
Ensuring data hasn't been changed. Tools: hashing, digital signatures.
Ensuring systems and data are up and reachable when needed. Tools: backups, redundancy, load balancing.
Proof of who did something so they can't deny it. Provided by digital signatures and audit trails.
Authentication (who are you), Authorization (what can you do), Accounting (what did you do).
Identification = claiming an identity (username, smart card). Authentication = proving it (password, PIN, biometric).
Give users only the minimum access needed to do their job.
AAA protocol for remote/network access; clients are wireless access points, switches, routers; uses a shared secret.
Cisco-created AAA protocol used to control administrator access to network devices (routers, switches, firewalls).
Successor to RADIUS used in modern mobile (4G/5G, LTE) networks.
Port-based network access control that authenticates devices (often with certificates) before they join the network.
Compares current security posture against a standard or framework to find the gaps between "as is" and "to be", then prioritizes and remediates them.
"Never trust, always verify": every user and device is verified every time, regardless of network location.
Where access decisions are made: policy engine, policy administrator, adaptive identity, threat scope reduction, policy-driven access control.
Where access is enforced and data moves: subject/system, policy enforcement point, implicit trust zones.
Zero trust component that decides whether to grant access, using policy plus context (SIEM, threat intel, user and device attributes).
Zero trust component that carries out the policy engine's decision, issues access tokens, and signals the enforcement point.
The gatekeeper in the data plane that allows, monitors, or ends the session.
Adjusting authentication and access based on context such as location, device, and behavior.
Shrinking the attack surface: fewer exposed services, less code, strict patching, least privilege.
Area of the network where components are trusted without re-verification (e.g. behind the PEP).
Network zone between the internet and internal LAN that hosts public-facing services; neither fully trusted nor untrusted.
Short posts that stop vehicles from reaching a building.
Detects changes in heat signature (people or animals).
Emits microwave pulses and detects frequency changes caused by movement.
Uses sound waves and their echo timing to detect movement, even around corners.
Detects force from someone stepping or touching.
A single decoy system that lures attackers so defenders can study their methods and protect real servers.
A network of honeypots that looks like a real network.
A bait file (e.g. passwords.txt) that triggers an alert when opened.
Fake data or credentials planted to detect misuse; any use triggers an alert.
Redirects DNS queries for malicious domains to a controlled address so malware can't reach its command server.
Record of every visitor's entry and exit; the person who signs a visitor in becomes responsible for them.
Group that evaluates, prioritizes, and approves or rejects proposed changes, including their security and financial impact.
Change management = the PROCESS of making changes safely. Configuration management = the recorded STATE of systems.
Making sure a change is authorized by the right people (and budget) before it happens, then documenting it.
The person accountable for a change being carried out properly, e.g. a project manager or the CISO for security tasks.
Anyone with an interest in or affected by the change: employees, customers, shareholders, suppliers, creditors/banks, regulators.
Assessing how a change could affect systems, security, and the business before it is made.
The plan to roll back a change if it fails.
Pre-approved, scheduled time (usually off-hours) to make changes with the least disruption.
Step-by-step written instructions so a task is done the same way every time.
Only listed apps/users/IPs are permitted; everything else is denied. Stops unknown malware from running.
Listed items are blocked; everything else is allowed. You must know and name what to block.
Actions blocked because they could cause vulnerabilities, e.g. unauthorized installs, direct access to critical servers.
Old software with outdated security and often no vendor support.
A service or component that must be running for another to work (e.g. IP Helper relies on five other components).
Tracks changes to code and documents (who, what, when) and allows rollback; provides an audit trail.
Time systems are offline for failure or maintenance; costs revenue and should be minimized.
Shared openly; used to ENCRYPT data for its owner and to VALIDATE their digital signatures.
Never shared; used to DECRYPT data and to CREATE digital signatures.
Use Mary's PUBLIC key. Only Mary's private key can decrypt it.
George signs with his PRIVATE key; anyone verifies with George's public key.
A trusted third party holds copies of keys so data can be recovered if a key is lost (often stored in an HSM).
Certificate file that contains the PRIVATE key (password-protected). Used to export/back up a cert with its key.
Certificate file with the PUBLIC key only (.p7b can hold a chain).
One shared key encrypts and decrypts; fast, used for bulk data. Examples: AES, DES, 3DES.
A public/private key pair; slow, used for key exchange and digital signatures. Examples: RSA, ECC, Diffie-Hellman.
Symmetric block cipher chosen by NIST in 2001; 128-, 192-, or 256-bit keys. The current standard.
Old symmetric ciphers: DES 56-bit, 3DES 168-bit. Weak/legacy.
Elliptic Curve Cryptography: asymmetric with small keys and low power use; ideal for mobile and IoT.
Key exchange method that lets two parties agree on a shared secret key over an insecure channel.
Encrypts fixed-size blocks of data; padding fills a block that isn't full.
Longer keys = more combinations = harder to brute-force, but more compute time.
How long a key stays in use before rotation; the book says typically one to two years.
Lets computations be performed on encrypted data without decrypting it.
Encrypts the whole drive; keys often stored in a TPM. Opal self-encrypting drives store keys on the drive itself.
BitLocker encrypts a volume and uses the TPM to store keys and check boot integrity.
Windows Encrypting File System encrypts individual files; keys are stored in the user's profile.
Encrypts individual records or fields in a database, each with its own key.
Protects data in transit, e.g. TLS for HTTPS; IPsec for VPNs.
Client and server agree on parameters, exchange keys and authenticate; then data is encrypted with a symmetric session key.
Trusted Platform Module: motherboard chip that stores keys, supports secure/measured boot and full-disk encryption.
Hardware Security Module: dedicated, tamper-resistant device that stores keys and performs crypto operations at scale (banks, CAs).
Software/cloud service that manages the key life cycle: generation, distribution, rotation, revocation.
Isolated hardware area of a processor (e.g. Apple T2 / Secure Enclave) that protects keys and biometric data from software attacks.
Making data or code deliberately hard to understand, e.g. to deter reverse engineering.
Hiding data inside other data such as images or audio files.
Replacing sensitive data (e.g. a card number) with a token of no value; the real value stays in a secure vault.
Replacing or hiding sensitive values with fictitious ones (e.g. XXX-XX-1234), often for test data.
One-way function producing a fixed-length digest; used for integrity and password storage. MD5 = 128-bit, SHA-1 = 160-bit.
Two different inputs producing the same hash value.
Adding random data to a password before hashing so identical passwords hash differently; defeats rainbow tables.
Hashing a password many times to slow brute-force attacks. Examples: PBKDF2, bcrypt.
Hash of a message signed with the sender's private key; gives integrity, authentication, and non-repudiation.
Decentralized ledger of blocks linked by hashes; tampering is evident because every copy would have to change.
The shared, transparent record of all blockchain transactions that anyone can verify.

cards.term: Proof of work / proof of stake
cards.def: Consensus mechanisms blockchain nodes use to agree a block is valid.
Trusted entity that issues and signs digital certificates. Online CAs issue in real time; offline (root) CAs stay isolated for security.
The self-signed root certificate at the top of the chain; every certificate must trace back to it.
Certificate Revocation List: list of revoked certificate serial numbers published by the CA; can be large and slow to download.
Online Certificate Status Protocol: real-time check of one certificate's status with the CA's responder; faster than a CRL.
Signed by its own owner, not a CA; fine for internal servers, not trusted by browsers.
Issued by a public CA (DigiCert, GlobalSign); needed for public e-commerce sites.
Certificate Signing Request: contains the requester's name, domain, and public key; sent to the CA to get a certificate.
One certificate for all hosts in a domain, e.g. *.securityplus.training covers web. and mail.
Fully qualified domain name: host + domain, e.g. web.securityplus.training.
Government-backed attacker with huge resources and high sophistication; motives: espionage, war, political influence.
Well-funded, highly skilled attacker (often nation-state) that breaks in and stays hidden for a long time, stealing data slowly.
Novice ("script kiddie") using off-the-shelf or dark-web tools; low sophistication but still damaging.
Attacker driven by political, social, or ideological causes; defaces websites, leaks data, runs DDoS.
Employee, contractor, or partner who misuses access, intentionally (revenge, money) or unintentionally (falls for phishing).
Criminal groups run like businesses for money: ransomware, card fraud, identity theft.
Technology used without IT approval (e.g. personal Dropbox, unapproved SaaS); not malicious but creates risk.
Internal attacks from inside with knowledge of systems; external relies on reconnaissance and social engineering.
Internal/external, resources/funding, sophistication/capability.
Stealing sensitive data to sell or use, e.g. personal, financial, or intellectual property.
Covert gathering of intelligence or trade secrets, typical of nation states.
Extortion using stolen or compromising data; ransomware is a form.
Finds and reports vulnerabilities to improve security, with permission.
Retaliation, often by disgruntled ex-employees (e.g. changing staff passwords after being fired).
Nation-state cyber operations to gain strategic advantage in conflict.
Vector = the path or method an attacker uses to get in (email, USB). Attack surface = all the points that could be attacked.
Untargeted deceptive emails or messages that trick many people into clicking links or giving data.
Phishing targeted at a specific person or group, e.g. the board of directors.
Phishing by SMS text message.
Phishing by voice call or voicemail, often with caller ID spoofing.
Faking the number shown on a call so it appears to come from a trusted source.
Malicious code or links hidden inside images (including steganography).
Malicious files (documents, executables) that run harmful code when opened.
Infected USB drives or external disks; e.g. a USB "dropped" in reception. Hand found USBs to security to open in a sandbox.
Vulnerability scanning with an agent installed on each host that reports to a central server.
Scanning hosts over the network with nothing installed (e.g. Nmap); what attackers use during reconnaissance.
Legacy or end-of-life software with no more patches; a prime target.
An open wireless network with no encryption; traffic can be sniffed in plaintext.
The Wi-Fi network name; disabling broadcast hides it from casual users (weak protection).
Only listed device MAC addresses may join the network (MACs can be spoofed).
Personal area network; easy pairing can allow unauthorized access. Turn it on only when needed.
Unneeded listening ports are entry points; scan regularly and close what isn't needed.
Factory usernames/passwords that attackers look up online; change them at install.
Compromising a weaker supplier, vendor, or MSP to reach their customers.
Third party that runs a company's IT; one breach can cascade to all its clients.
Manipulating people ("hacking the human") using trust, urgency, fear, or greed.
Misinformation = false info spread without intent to mislead. Disinformation = deliberately false info.
Pretending to be a trusted person (police, help desk, executive).
Using a real compromised business email account for fraud, e.g. changing bank details on an invoice.
Inventing a believable scenario to extract information (e.g. fake tech support call).
Compromising a website a target group regularly visits so their devices get infected.
Fake emails or sites that copy a trusted brand (bank, Microsoft) to steal data.
Registering look-alike misspelled domains (e.g. gooogle.com) to catch typing errors.
Mock phishing campaigns sent to staff, followed by remedial training for anyone who falls for it.
Inserting malicious code into a running program's memory to execute arbitrary commands (e.g. Code Red worm, 2001).
Sending more data than a buffer can hold so it overwrites adjacent memory and can run attacker code (e.g. SQL Slammer, 2003). Fix: input validation, safe languages, memory protection.
Two threads/processes access the same data at once and the outcome depends on timing (e.g. two people booking the last airline seat).
Time-of-check/time-of-use: data changes between when it's checked and when it's used.
A legitimate-looking software update carrying hidden malware (e.g. CCleaner 2017). Defense: verify digital signatures and sources.
Flaw in the operating system's code or configuration (e.g. BlueKeep RDP flaw in Windows).
Malicious SQL entered into input fields to manipulate a database query, e.g. ' OR 1=1 --. Fix: input validation, parameterized queries/prepared statements, stored procedures.
Injecting malicious script (<script> tags, JavaScript) into a web page so it runs in other users' browsers; steals cookies/sessions. Fix: input validation and output encoding.
Flaw in the low-level software that controls hardware; fix with firmware updates.
Product no longer made or supported: no patches, parts, or warranty (e.g. Windows XP after April 8, 2014).
Outdated technology still in use because it's critical; lacks modern security and vendor focus.
Attacker breaks out of a virtual machine to reach the hypervisor, host, or other VMs.
Uncontrolled creation of VMs that nobody manages or patches.
Disks or memory reused between VMs without sanitizing, leaking data; or one VM exhausting shared resources.
Many customers on the same physical hardware; poor isolation can enable side-channel access between tenants.
Exposed storage buckets, open ports, or overly broad permissions caused by misunderstood cloud settings.
Cloud Access Security Broker: enforces security policy between users and cloud services and gives visibility across cloud apps.
List of all components and libraries used to build software, so their vulnerabilities can be tracked.
Reused code libraries may contain vulnerabilities or malware.
If a certificate authority is breached, attackers can issue fraudulent trusted certificates.
Theft or weak generation of a key, letting attackers decrypt or forge data.
Extracting secrets from leakage like power use, timing, or electromagnetic emissions.
Predictable random numbers produce weak, guessable keys.
Attacker downgrades a victim's HTTPS session to plain HTTP to read data (an HTTPS downgrade attack).
Forcing a connection to fall back to an older, weaker protocol or cipher (e.g. POODLE against old SSL).
Padding Oracle On Downgraded Legacy Encryption: man-in-the-middle attack that forces SSL 3.0.
Security holes from setup errors: default credentials, open ports, permissive firewall rules, excessive privileges.
Removing iOS (Apple) restrictions to gain full control; weakens device security.
Removing Android restrictions to gain root access; weakens device security.
Installing apps from outside the official app store (e.g. Android APK files).
Central control of mobile devices: password policies, remote wipe, updates, disabling camera or features.
A flaw unknown to the vendor with no patch available (e.g. Stuxnet used four zero-days).
Grayware bundled with other downloads; not clearly malicious but slows the system.
Malware that encrypts files and demands payment (usually cryptocurrency) for the key.
Malware disguised as legitimate software; often installs a backdoor.
Trojan that gives the attacker remote command-and-control of the infected computer.
Self-replicating malware that spreads across networks on its own, consuming bandwidth (e.g. NIMDA, 2001).
Covertly tracks user activity (e.g. via tracking cookies) and sends data to third parties.
Unneeded preinstalled software that wastes storage and resources; not necessarily malware.
Malware that attaches to files or boot sectors and needs user action to spread.
Malware that runs only in memory, piggybacking on legitimate programs, leaving few files on disk.
Changes its code with each infection to evade signature-based detection.
Records keystrokes to capture passwords and card numbers.
Dormant code that triggers at a set time or event (e.g. when an employee is removed from payroll).
Malware with kernel/root-level access that hides itself and other malware by hooking system calls.
Isolated environment (e.g. VM, Cuckoo) used to safely detonate and analyze suspicious files or test patches.
Breaking in with force (crowbar, sledgehammer); not the same as password brute force.
Copying a badge's RFID signal to make a duplicate; skimming uses a fake reader. Counter with MFA (e.g. biometric + card).
Using or causing power outages, floods, or fire to disrupt systems.
Using a compromised host as a stepping stone to attack other internal systems (lateral movement).
Mapping hosts, OS and software versions, ports and services (e.g. with Nmap).
DoS = attack from one host; DDoS = from many hosts (a botnet).
Network of malware-infected devices (bots) controlled by an attacker, often used for DDoS.
DoS that sends many SYNs but never completes the TCP handshake (no ACK), leaving half-open connections.
Small request triggers a much larger response aimed at the victim (e.g. Smurf with ICMP, DNS amplification).
Attacker spoofs the victim's IP so third-party servers send their responses to the victim.
ICMP echo requests sent to a broadcast address with the victim's spoofed IP, flooding the victim with replies.
Fake ARP messages map the victim's IP to the attacker's MAC on a LAN, redirecting traffic (Layer 2, local only).
Planting fake DNS records so users are redirected to a malicious site.
1) local DNS cache, 2) HOSTS file, 3) DNS servers/root hints.
Adds digital signatures to DNS records to prevent cache poisoning.
View and clear the local DNS cache.
Unauthorized wireless access point on a network (e.g. a Raspberry Pi) used to intercept traffic.
Fake access point with the same or similar SSID as a legitimate one; sign: you can't reach company resources.
Sending forged deauth/disassociation frames to knock devices off Wi-Fi.
Illegal radio interference that blocks wireless access (wireless DoS).
Changing a device's MAC address to impersonate an authorized device.
Man-in-the-middle: attacker intercepts, reads, or alters traffic between two parties.
Stealing a session token/cookie (via XSS, MITM, man-in-the-browser) to take over a logged-in session.
Capturing data and resending it later; Kerberos prevents it with sequence numbers and timestamps.
Capturing credentials (e.g. Telnet cleartext, NTLM) and reusing them. Use SSH instead of Telnet; avoid NTLM.
Trying passwords leaked from one site on many other sites, exploiting password reuse.
Script on the victim that connects back to the attacker's machine and gives them a command line (e.g. bash -i >& /dev/tcp/ip/port).
Untrusted input inserted into an application so it runs unintended commands (SQLi, XSS). SELECT * or 1=1 in logs suggests SQLi.
Windows protection that blocks code from running in non-executable memory, mitigating buffer overflows.
Exploiting a flaw to gain higher rights than authorized (e.g. user to admin).
Cross-site request forgery: tricks a logged-in user's browser into sending an unwanted request to a site.
Server-side request forgery: tricks a server into making requests to internal systems on the attacker's behalf.
Using ../ (or %2f) in a path to access files outside the web root, e.g. /etc/passwd or /etc/shadow.
Linux file holding password hashes; a prime target for offline cracking.
Predefined SQL script; the book calls it the best defense against SQL injection, with input validation second.
Creating two different inputs with the same hash, e.g. to swap a signed benign document for a malicious one.
Exploits the birthday paradox to find hash collisions; defend with longer hashes (avoid MD5).
Using a captured NTLM password hash to authenticate without knowing the password. Defense: Kerberos, disable NTLM.
Trying words from a dictionary list; defeated by passwords with misspellings/special characters.
Trying a few common passwords against many accounts to avoid lockouts.
Trying every combination, often with rainbow tables; indicator: many accounts locked out. Defense: lockout, salting.
Combination of dictionary and brute-force (e.g. words plus numbers/symbols).
Online = guessing against a live login (logged, lockouts). Offline = cracking a stolen hash file (SAM, /etc/shadow) with no alerts.
Early sign of an attack in progress, e.g. account lockouts, impossible travel, unusual resource use.
Logins from two distant locations in an unrealistically short time, suggesting account compromise.
Unusually many simultaneous sessions for one account, suggesting compromise.
Logs generated at unusual times, possibly from attacker activity or tampering.
Gaps in expected logs, a sign of tampering to hide activity.
Access-denied or DLP block events showing attempts to reach protected data.
Dividing a network into isolated segments to limit lateral movement and contain breaches.
Separating networks with separate routers, switches, and firewalls (an air gap is the extreme).
Logical network segment created on a switch; groups devices by department/function and reduces broadcast traffic.
Dividing an IP network into smaller subnets with subnet masks for management and security.
Security policy applied to individual workloads or devices; common in data centers and cloud.
Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard: rules for protecting credit card data; cardholder systems should be segmented.
US law protecting the privacy and security of Protected Health Information (PHI).
Rules on a router/firewall (or file system) that allow or deny traffic or access.
A new firewall/router starts with a "deny all" rule; access is granted only by adding allow rules.
What an authorized user can do with a resource: read, write, execute, delete.
Only approved applications may run; blocks games and unknown malware alike.
Specific named applications are prevented from running (e.g. via Microsoft AppLocker).
Separating critical systems or infected devices into self-contained environments.
Applying vendor updates to fix vulnerabilities; mandatory, not optional.
Security Information and Event Management: centralizes and correlates logs in real time and alerts the SOC.
Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response: uses playbooks (and AI/ML) to automatically respond to incidents.
Predefined set of automated actions and workflows for responding to a specific incident type.
Making systems follow approved secure configurations (baselines such as CIS Benchmarks), detecting and fixing drift automatically.
Industry-standard secure configuration baselines for OSes, cloud, and applications.
Retiring unneeded assets: update the asset register, document it, and sanitize the data.
Inventory of all hardware, software, and digital assets; updated when assets are decommissioned.
Burning > pulping > shredding (use a cross-cut shredder).
Shredding > pulverizing > degaussing. All destroy the media; to reuse it, overwrite/wipe/format instead.
Erasing magnetic media (hard drives, tapes) with a strong magnetic field; doesn't work on SSDs.
Reducing a system's attack surface: encryption, endpoint protection, closing ports, changing defaults, removing unneeded software.
Endpoint Detection and Response: continuous monitoring, behavioral analysis, alerts, isolation and remediation, forensics on endpoints.
Host-based Intrusion Prevention System: monitors and blocks malicious activity on a single host.
Software firewall on an individual device; protects laptops away from the office.
Unencrypted remote access (cleartext passwords); replace with SSH (port 22).
Windows file and print sharing ports; should be blocked from the internet.
Multi-tenant cloud: many customers share the provider's hardware. Cheapest; risk of one tenant affecting another.
Single-tenant cloud dedicated to one organization; more control and security.
Organizations in the same industry share a cloud and the cost of a bespoke application.
Mix of on-premises and cloud infrastructure.
Infrastructure as a Service: provider supplies hardware (servers, storage, network); customer installs, configures, and patches the OS and apps.
Platform as a Service: provider supplies an environment for developers to build and deploy apps (e.g. Azure App Service).
Software as a Service: finished application accessed over the web (e.g. Office 365, Salesforce); customer can't modify it.
Security as a Service: security functions (e.g. identity and access management, managed security staff) delivered from the cloud.
Anything as a Service: other cloud services such as Desktop, Network, or Backup as a Service.
Defines which security tasks belong to the cloud provider (e.g. physical security) and which to the customer (e.g. application security, data, configuration).
Data management, latency, lack of synchronization between on-prem and cloud, and maintenance overhead.
Data breaches, vulnerabilities introduced by their software, compliance failures, and operational disruption (e.g. Target breach via HVAC contractor).
Defining infrastructure in machine-readable code (YAML, JSON) with tools like Terraform or Ansible; consistent, repeatable, version-controlled.
Cloud provider runs and scales the servers; developers deploy code only. Customer still owns app and data security. Often uses Backend as a Service.
Application split into small independent services that talk over APIs; a failure in one is isolated.
Application programming interface: defined way for software components or microservices to talk to each other.
Switches, VLANs, wireless access points; MAC addresses and ARP.
Routers and layer 3 switches; IP addresses and routing.
Load balancer (TCP/UDP).
Web application firewall (WAF) and NIPS; protocols like HTTP, DNS, SMTP, SMB, FTP.
Route a router uses when it has no specific route, usually toward the ISP.
Switch table mapping MAC addresses to ports.
Web application firewall: protects web servers and apps from attacks like SQLi and XSS (layer 7).
Network intrusion prevention system: monitors network traffic and blocks attacks inline using signatures, anomalies, behavior.
Physically isolated system with no wired or wireless connection; data moves only on removable media.
Dividing a network by software rules (subnets, VLANs with tags) instead of physical separation.
Separates the control plane (central controller decides) from the data plane (devices forward); management plane monitors. Programmable, dynamic security.
Infrastructure in the organization's own building; full control, good for strict compliance, low latency, and legacy systems.
Centralized = decisions at the top (e.g. McDonald's). Decentralized = authority spread out (e.g. Toyota regions; blockchain).
Packaging an app with its code, libraries, and dependencies so it runs the same anywhere (e.g. Docker); containers share the host OS kernel.
Pool of identical virtual desktops accessed by thin clients; corrupted VMs are simply replaced.
Running an app isolated from the OS (e.g. Microsoft App-V).
Lack of standards, privacy, insecure communication, short vendor support, physical tampering, supply chain, weak user awareness (default passwords).
Industrial control systems that monitor and control physical processes (energy, water, manufacturing); targeted by Stuxnet.
Programmable logic controller: SCADA level 1 device that reads sensors and controls actuators.
Human-machine interface: operator screens for monitoring and controlling an industrial process.
Real-time operating system that guarantees tasks run within strict time limits (e.g. flight control).
Specialized computer inside a product, e.g. car engine control units, ABS, smart thermostats.
Systems stay up despite failures; 99.999% uptime, about 5 minutes of downtime a year.
Cloud data copied across zones and regions (e.g. Azure GZRS) so one data center outage doesn't stop service.
How quickly an organization recovers from a critical failure.
Scalability = ability to add resources as demand grows; elasticity = automatically scaling up and down.
Moving risk to a third party, e.g. an SLA that obliges the provider to fix a crashed database within 2 hours.
When a system can't be patched (vendor contract, critical app); needs compensating controls.
UPS keeps power long enough for graceful shutdown; a managed power distribution unit distributes and monitors power remotely.
Processing data close to where it's created or used to reduce latency.
Full cost of a system: purchase, maintenance, support, and SLAs.
Multiple layers of security so one failure doesn't expose everything.
WAN/internet = untrusted; screened subnet (DMZ) = boundary layer; LAN = trusted. Firewalls sit between each.
Router + ACL at the WAN edge; reverse proxy, load balancer, jump server in the screened subnet; IDS/IPS, sensors, switches, forward proxy inside.
Network segments with their own policies, access controls, and trust levels (e.g. separate zones for DB and file servers).
All points an attacker could use: endpoints, network services, ports/protocols, accounts, third-party integrations, cloud, people.
One component whose failure takes down the whole system; avoid with redundancy.
On failure, the device blocks everything (secure, but stops service). E.g. a bank door that locks on power loss.
On failure, the device allows everything through (keeps service up, but a security risk).
Active devices act on threats (firewall, IPS). Passive devices only observe and alert (IDS).
Inline devices sit in the traffic path (firewall, IPS, load balancer). Tap/monitor devices copy traffic for analysis (packet sniffer, IDS via SPAN/tap).
Hardened intermediary host admins connect to (via SSH/RDP) before managing internal servers and devices.
Makes internet requests on behalf of internal users; does URL filtering, content filtering, caching, and logging.
Sits in the screened subnet and handles incoming requests from the internet to internal servers; can authenticate and decrypt to filter.
IPS is inline and blocks attacks; IDS is passive and only alerts. Network versions = NIPS/NIDS; host versions = HIPS/HIDS.
Distributes traffic across servers for performance and fault tolerance. Layer 4 uses headers (IP/port); layer 7 uses content.
Layer 7 scheduling that sends requests to the least busy server.
Load balancer sends a client (by IP) to the same server every time.
Rotates requests across servers in order; can't tell if a server is down.
Collects and analyzes traffic for anomalies; feeds IDSs.
Controls what can connect to switch ports: sticky MAC, disabling unused ports, 802.1X.
Switch learns and locks the first MAC address on a port; other devices on that port are denied.
Supplicant (device asking for access), authenticator (switch/AP), authentication server (RADIUS).
Extensible Authentication Protocol framework used by 802.1X; methods include EAP-TLS (certificates), PEAP, EAP-MD5.
Web application firewall (layer 7) protecting web apps from SQLi, XSS, and DDoS.
Unified threat management: all-in-one firewall with malware inspection, DLP, content and URL filtering.
Next-generation firewall: layer 7 application awareness, deep packet inspection, IPS, TLS inspection, cloud threat intel, user behavior monitoring.
Filters by IP, port, and protocol (book calls it stateless); no deep packet inspection.
Inspects application-layer content to control specific apps and users (deep packet inspection).
Encrypted tunnel over the internet to the company network. L2TP/IPsec is more secure than PPTP/SSL; HTML5 (clientless) VPNs are easy but less secure.
Secure remote command-line access (port 22) that replaces Telnet; can use key pairs (ssh-keygen, authorized_keys).
Microsoft Remote Desktop Protocol for Windows machines only; users must be in the Remote Desktop Users group.
Authentication Header: provides integrity and authentication of the packet (hashing), not encryption.
Encapsulating Security Payload: encrypts the data (AES/3DES/DES) and provides confidentiality.
Internet Key Exchange: sets up IPsec using Diffie-Hellman over UDP port 500.
Encrypts the entire original packet; used for remote-access and site-to-site VPNs.
Encrypts only the payload; used for host-to-host communication inside a network.
Permanent VPN connecting two offices' networks.
Software-defined WAN: centrally managed, encrypted connections between branches, data centers, and cloud, routing by application needs.
Secure Access Service Edge: cloud-delivered networking plus security (zero trust, IAM, IPS, content filtering) wherever users are.
Preventative at the perimeter (firewalls, IPS, ACLs). Detective inside the network (IDS, SIEM, log analyzers).
Data governed by specific laws: PII, PHI, financial, legal, government, consumer data.
Personally Identifiable Information: data unique to a person, e.g. SSN, driver's license number, biometrics, phone, email.
Protected Health Information: a person's medical history, test results, and treatments; regulated by HIPAA.
Creative innovations protected by law: patents, copyrights, trademarks, trade secrets.
Confidential business information that gives a competitive edge; protected by NDAs, contracts, and access restrictions.
Data generated by the company itself, such as research and product development.
Human-readable = text, images, audio. Non-human-readable = binary, machine code, encrypted data.
EU regulation protecting personal data and privacy rights.
California Consumer Privacy Act: California consumer data rights.
Sarbanes-Oxley Act: US law requiring financial transparency and accountability for public companies.
Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act: US privacy and security rules for financial institutions.
Top secret > secret > confidential > unclassified.
Confidential/proprietary > private > sensitive > public.
Data whose disclosure would damage the company (R&D, legal); access needs authorization.
Limited-access data with legal, regulatory, or policy constraints on its use.
Information available to anyone (brochures, published news).
Data the organization needs to operate, e.g. backups and encryption keys.
Stored data on disks, databases, or file servers. Protect with FDE, database encryption.
Data moving across a network. Protect with TLS/HTTPS, VPNs.
Data being processed in RAM (volatile); a crash can dump it to a .dmp file.
Data is subject to the laws of the country where it was created/stored and can't simply be moved elsewhere.
Determining a user's or device's physical location to verify that access requests are legitimate.
Limiting data access to users or devices in specific regions.
MD5 = 128-bit, SHA-1 = 160-bit, SHA-256 = 256-bit, SHA-512 = 512-bit, SHA-3 = 224 to 512-bit.
Logical operation: same bits = 0, different bits = 1; used in simple obfuscation and in many ciphers.
Caesar-style substitution that shifts each letter 13 places (TIME FOR TEA -> GVZR SBE GRN); applying it twice restores the text.
Limiting who can read or change data based on role and privileges.
The single front-end IP address users connect to for a load-balanced farm or cluster.
Two or more load balancers all handling traffic; if one fails, the others carry the full load (performance may drop).
One active load balancer; a passive standby monitors it and takes over on failure.
Load balancing spreads requests across many servers; clustering makes several nodes act as one system with failover.
Shared storage in a cluster holding configuration and state that all nodes access.
Impartial cluster member that helps decide cluster state and prevents split-brain.
Regular status signal between cluster nodes; if the active node's heartbeat stops, the passive node takes over.
Fully equipped, staffed, real-time replicated recovery site; fastest recovery, most expensive.
Equipped recovery site with data a few hours behind; moderate cost and recovery time.
Empty shell with power and water but no equipment, staff, or data; cheapest, slowest recovery.
Spreading data centers far apart so one disaster can't take everything down.
Locally redundant storage: 3 copies in one data center. Cheapest; lost if that site fails.
Zone-redundant storage: copies across 3 availability zones in one region; no protection from a regional disaster.
Geo-redundant storage: 3 local copies in the primary region plus a copy in a distant secondary region.
Geo-zone-redundant storage: copies across 3 zones in the primary region plus a secondary region; most resilient.
Using different vendors/technologies (e.g. two firewall brands) so one flaw doesn't defeat everything.
Using several cloud providers for resilience and to avoid vendor lock-in; adds complexity and consistency challenges.
Being so dependent on one provider that moving away is hard or costly.
Plan to keep essential functions running during and after a disruption: redundancy, communication plans, trained people, regular reviews.
Making sure people, technology, and infrastructure can meet current and future demand.
Identifying future leaders so key roles transition smoothly.
Discussion-based walkthrough of a disaster scenario around a table; the easiest test to set up.
Verifying operations switch to backup systems or sites with minimal downtime.
Realistic exercise of an incident scenario, overseen and scored by a white team.
Running backup systems simultaneously with production to confirm they work.
Copies all data. Most storage and slowest to back up, but restores from one set.
Backs up changes since the last backup of any kind. Fastest/smallest backup; restore needs the full + every incremental.
Backs up changes since the last full backup; grows daily. Restore needs only the full + the latest differential.
Backup copy kept far enough away (different power supplier) to survive a local disaster.
Point-in-time copy of a VM, including memory state; quickest way to roll a VM back.
Real-time copying of data to another location (cloud or hot site).
Recording every change (create, edit, delete) so data can be restored to an exact point in time; e.g. Exchange journal mailboxes.
Backup power source for extended outages.
Uninterruptible power supply: battery power for a few minutes so servers can shut down gracefully.
Power distribution unit: distributes power, protects against spikes/brownouts, and can be monitored remotely.
Approved set of secure configurations that is the starting point for every system: establish, deploy, maintain.
Security Technical Implementation Guide: US DoD hardening guidelines for systems and networks.
Microsoft tool to push and enforce security settings across Windows devices, preventing configuration drift.
Platform-agnostic repository of modules for deploying baselines across Windows, Linux, and macOS.
Uses the Security Content Automation Protocol to compare system settings against a checklist (NIST etc.) and report non-compliance.
CIS Configuration Assessment Tool: scans systems against CIS Benchmarks.
Change default creds, port security, VLANs, SSH (not Telnet), disable unused ports, secure SNMP, ACLs, firmware updates.
Change default passwords, enable firewall, disable or SSH-only remote management, firmware updates, ACLs, secure SNMP, logging, locked rack.
Change default admin password and SSID, disable SSID broadcast, MAC filtering, use WPA3.
Change defaults, strong device authentication, firmware updates, segment IoT on its own network.
Assessment of a location for interference (walls, microwaves, elevators, metal) to decide where to place wireless access points.
Visual map of wireless signal strength used to find coverage gaps and failing access points.
Bring Your Own Device: personal devices used for work; needs containerization to separate work and personal data.
Choose Your Own Device: employee picks from a list of company-approved, company-owned devices.
Corporate-Owned, Personally Enabled: company device that can also be used personally under company policy; full device encryption.
Separating corporate apps and data from personal data on the same mobile device.
MDM command that erases a lost or stolen device back to factory settings.
Two wireless devices connected directly without an access point (e.g. Wi-Fi Direct).
Web page that must be completed (login, email, accept AUP) before Wi-Fi gives internet access; e.g. airports, hotels.
Wi-Fi Protected Setup: push-button connection to Wi-Fi; convenient but has known weaknesses.
Pre-shared key: the shared Wi-Fi passphrase (e.g. the password a restaurant gives you).
Sending unsolicited messages to nearby discoverable Bluetooth devices.
Stealing data (contacts, messages, files) from a Bluetooth device without permission.
Low-power Bluetooth for wearables and IoT; uses random device addresses to prevent tracking.
Near-field communication: very short-range (centimeters) contactless communication, e.g. Apple Pay. Use an RFID-blocking wallet against skimming.
Copying a phone's SIM to hijack its number; a cellular network risk.
Radio-frequency identification tags for asset tracking, anti-theft, and proximity cards.
Sharing a phone's cellular internet connection with another device such as a laptop.
Old Wi-Fi encryption using RC4 with a 24-bit IV that is reused; easily cracked. Never use.
Replaced WEP; still RC4 but TKIP changes keys dynamically. Obsolete.
Wi-Fi encryption using AES with CCMP (128-bit). Personal mode uses a PSK; still common.
Current Wi-Fi standard (2018): SAE replaces PSK, protected management frames, 192-bit Enterprise mode, Enhanced Open.
Simultaneous Authentication of Equals: WPA3 key exchange that resists offline brute-force attacks and provides perfect forward secrecy.
Each session uses a unique key, so a stolen long-term key can't decrypt past sessions.
WPA3 feature protecting management frames from spoofing (e.g. deauthentication attacks).
Encrypts open (no-password) public Wi-Fi to stop eavesdropping.
Connecting IoT devices to Wi-Fi by scanning a QR code.
The device that forwards authentication requests to the RADIUS server: VPN, wireless AP, 802.1X switch (not the user's PC).
Protected EAP: encrypts EAP in a TLS tunnel using a certificate on the server only.
Most secure EAP method: certificates on both the server and the client/device.
Tunnels with a server certificate first, then authenticates the client's credentials inside the tunnel.
Cisco EAP method that uses a Protected Access Credential (PAC) instead of certificates.
Checking all input against allowed formats and ranges; prevents SQLi, buffer overflow, integer overflow.
Cookies protected (e.g. Secure, HttpOnly flags, encrypted) so session tokens can't be stolen.
Reviewing source code for vulnerabilities without running it.
Digitally signing software so users can verify its publisher and that it hasn't been altered.
Open Worldwide Application Security Project: secure coding guidance and the OWASP Top 10 web risks.
Modern browsers isolate each tab/process so malicious code in one can't affect the rest.
Buying assets: CAB approval, vendor vetting, total cost of ownership, risk assessment, compliance alignment.
Vetting suppliers' security, track record, and compliance, not just price. Buy only from reputable vendors.
Record of all assets with location, value, and owner; a device on the network that isn't in it is likely rogue.
Consistent asset names (PC1, DC1, SQL1) matching DNS hostnames; a device with a nonstandard name stands out as rogue.
Named owner accountable for an asset's condition, use, and security.
Categorizing assets as critical, essential, or non-essential to set support priority and protection level.
Up-to-date list of hardware, software, and licenses; tools include IBM Maximo and ServiceNow.
Configuration management database: central repository of IT assets and their configurations (e.g. ServiceNow).
Assigning unique identifiers to assets and discovering them: asset tags, barcodes/QR, RFID, GPS/AirTags, MDM/Intune, Nmap.
Removing all data before disposal or reuse: overwriting/wiping, secure erase, degaussing. Sanitized devices can be donated.
Built-in drive command that permanently removes data (important for SSDs).
Shredding, incineration, pulverization, crushing, chemical decomposition, pulping (paper).
Documentation from a disposal vendor proving assets were destroyed according to legal and policy requirements.
Policy for how long data must be kept before disposal (e.g. US medical data at least 6 years; IRS suggests 7 years for tax records).
Vulnerability scan with no login; sees only what's visible from the network, like an external attacker.
Vulnerability scan that logs in with privileges; more accurate and sees patches, configs, accounts, and third-party software.
Widely used network vulnerability scanner supporting credentialed and non-credentialed scans.
Security Content Automation Protocol: framework letting scanners check systems against a configuration baseline.
Open Vulnerability and Assessment Language: XML schema describing a system's security state and vulnerabilities (part of SCAP).
Extensible Configuration Checklist Description Format: XML format for machine-readable configuration checklists (part of SCAP).
Examining source code or binaries for flaws without running them.
Testing an application while it runs to see how it behaves under attack (e.g. fuzzing).
Tool that sends crafted requests to web apps to find SQLi, XSS, misconfigurations, and authentication flaws.
Tracking the libraries/components your software uses against vulnerability databases.
Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures: MITRE's list giving each public vulnerability a unique ID, e.g. CVE-2023-5752.
National Vulnerability Database (NIST): enriches CVEs with severity scores and details.
Real-time stream of threat data from vendors, governments (CISA), OSINT, or commercial providers.
Open-source intelligence: threat information from public sources such as websites, forums, news, government reports, blogs.
Proprietary = your own internal intel; third-party = from vendors (e.g. Recorded Future), communities, or governments.
Structured Threat Information eXpression: standard format (by MITRE) for describing threat intelligence.
Trusted Automated eXchange of Intelligence Information: protocol that transports STIX data over HTTPS.
Search engine for internet-connected devices showing open ports, services, and vulnerabilities.
Evidence an attack happened: malicious IPs, malware hashes, suspicious URLs.
Tactics, techniques, and procedures: how a threat actor operates.
Knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques.
Information Sharing and Analysis Center: sector-specific threat sharing group (FS-ISAC, H-ISAC, E-ISAC; MS-ISAC for state/local government).
Hidden part of the internet reached through Tor; monitored for stolen data and attacker chatter.
White-box test: testers get full information about the systems.
Gray-box test: testers get some information.
Black-box test: testers get no information, like an outside attacker.
Invites ethical (authorized) hackers to report vulnerabilities instead of exploiting them.
Program that pays outside researchers rewards for vulnerabilities they find; cheaper than a pen test.
Scanner reports a vulnerability that isn't really there.
Scanner misses a real vulnerability. The more dangerous error.
Scanner finding confirmed by manual inspection.
Common Vulnerability Scoring System: 0.1-3.9 low, 4.0-6.9 medium, 7.0-8.9 high, 9.0-10.0 critical.
Percentage of an asset's value that would be lost if a vulnerability is exploited.
Organization-specific factors (infrastructure, industry, regulations, legacy systems) that change a vulnerability's real severity.
How much risk an organization is willing to bear; guides how fast vulnerabilities must be fixed.
Financial coverage for losses from cyber incidents; transfers risk but doesn't replace security.
Documented, risk-assessed decision not to remediate a vulnerability yet (e.g. a system that can't be patched).
Confirming fixes worked: rescanning, auditing the process, and ongoing verification.
Management report with overview, CVSS breakdown, remediation progress, risk reduction metrics, and recommendations.
Text record of events on a device; an audit trail for troubleshooting and investigations.
Records authorized and unauthorized access to resources and privileges (e.g. Windows Security event log).
Software on a network device that reports data to an SNMP manager.
Central system that polls agents using GET, GETNEXT, and SET on the Management Information Base (MIB).
Management Information Base: database of the information an SNMP device exposes.
Unsolicited alert an SNMP agent sends to the manager when a threshold or event occurs (e.g. hardware failure).
Network management system: shows device status (green up, yellow warning, red down) from SNMP data.
NIDS passively monitors traffic and alerts. NIPS sits inline and actively blocks malicious traffic.
Collecting and normalizing logs from many sources into one place (usually a SIEM) for correlation.
Rules and thresholds that notify the SOC when specific events occur.
Turning monitoring data into dashboards, compliance reports, and executive summaries.
Long-term storage of logs and data for investigations, forensics, and compliance; SIEMs use log rotation to move old data to archives.
Isolating a possibly compromised system or file so it can't infect others; can be automatic or manual.
Adjusting thresholds and rules to cut false positives without causing false negatives. Too many alerts on day one = thresholds misconfigured.
Agent = software on each endpoint sends data to the SIEM. Agentless = gathers data remotely via protocols (SNMP, WMI, ICMP, HTTP) or network sensors.
Data collection, aggregation (removing duplicates), correlation across sources, alerting and reporting.
Scans for malware signatures and suspicious behavior; deletes or quarantines detections.
Data loss prevention: outbound tool that uses pattern matching (e.g. regex for card numbers) to block PII or sensitive data leaving by email, upload, or USB.
Collects metadata about traffic flows (source/destination IP, ports, protocol) to spot anomalies and bandwidth hogs; IPFIX is the IETF standard.
Vulnerability scanners comparing systems against CIS Benchmarks and scoring findings with CVSS.
Stateful tracks connection state (knows if a packet belongs to an established session). Stateless filters each packet by rules only (IP, port, protocol).
Inbound rules control traffic coming into the network; outbound rules control what internal hosts can reach.
Explicit deny = a specific rule blocking something (place these first). Implicit deny = the final default "deny all" that blocks anything not allowed.
Rules are processed top-down; the first match wins, so a broad block above an allow rule overrides it.
Matches a single host IP; used for port-forwarding rules to one server.
SYN -> SYN-ACK -> ACK. TCP is connection-oriented and reliable.
Connectionless and faster but no delivery guarantee; used for streaming, gaming, DNS queries, VoIP.
0-1023 (e.g. 80 HTTP, 443 HTTPS, 25 SMTP).
49152-65535; ephemeral ports assigned to client sessions.
Two firewalls create WAN / screened subnet / LAN zones; a three-legged firewall does the same with one device.
IDS/IPS/AV match traffic against known attack patterns; misses new attacks and depends on updates.
Flags deviations from a learned baseline of normal behavior; can catch zero-days but has more false positives.
Watching alert patterns over time to spot targeted attacks and tune out false positives.
Agent-based, centralized proxy, URL scanning, content categorization, block rules, reputation-based filtering.
Windows prompt requiring consent or admin credentials before system changes.
Applies GPOs at domain or OU level, e.g. account lockout threshold of 3, software deployment, AppLocker.
Group Policy feature that allows or blocks applications on Windows (replaced Software Restriction Policies).
Security-Enhanced Linux: kernel-level mandatory access control (MAC) with strict policies.
Linux Unified Key Setup: Linux full-disk encryption.
Port 21, unencrypted file transfer. Secure replacements: SFTP (22) or FTPS (989/990).
Port 23, unencrypted remote access. Replace with SSH (22).
SMTP port 25 (unencrypted mail transfer). Secure submission port 587 (STARTTLS) or 465 (implicit TLS).
DNS uses port 53 (UDP for queries, TCP for zone transfers). DNSSEC digitally signs records (RRSIG) to stop poisoning.
UDP 67/68, automatic IP addressing.
UDP 69, trivial file transfer with no authentication.
HTTP port 80 (cleartext). HTTPS port 443 (TLS-encrypted).
POP3 110, POP3S 995. Downloads mail and removes it from the server.
IMAP 143, IMAPS 993. Keeps mail on the server.
Port 123 (UDP), time synchronization; Kerberos needs clocks within 5 minutes.
SNMP UDP 161 (queries) and 162 (traps). Use SNMPv3: authenticated and encrypted, no default "public" community string.
LDAP 389 (cleartext directory queries). LDAPS 636 encrypts with TLS; use it for Active Directory.
Port 88. Ticket-based authentication (TGT then service tickets); uses timestamps and sequence numbers to stop replay; replaces NTLM; time skew over 5 minutes breaks it.
All port 22. SSH = secure remote shell; SCP = secure copy (Linux); SFTP = secure file transfer over SSH.
Port 445, Windows file and printer sharing; keep internal.
UDP 500.
Port 3389, Microsoft remote desktop.
SIP 5060 (5061 with TLS) sets up VoIP calls; SRTP encrypts the voice/video stream.
Uses PKI certificates to encrypt and digitally sign email; hard to scale because users must exchange certificates.
End-to-end email encryption with key pairs, without a PKI/CA.
DNS TXT record listing which IP addresses may send mail for a domain; stops spoofing.
Digitally signs outgoing email so the receiver can verify it came from the domain and wasn't altered.
Policy telling receivers what to do (none, quarantine, reject) when SPF/DKIM checks fail, plus reporting.
Filters inbound and outbound mail for spam, malware, malicious URLs/attachments, and DLP.
Blocks requests to malicious or disallowed domains at the DNS lookup stage.
Baselines critical files and alerts on unauthorized changes; Windows has sfc /scannow.
Network access control: checks device health (patches, AV) before granting LAN access; non-compliant devices go to a quarantine network with a remediation server.
Permanent agent stays installed; dissolvable (temporary/agentless) agent runs a one-time check.
Extended detection and response: correlates data from endpoints, network, email, and cloud (beyond EDR's endpoint focus).
Uses machine learning to baseline normal user behavior and flag anomalies, e.g. insider threats.
Creating accounts and assigning access based on job role after background checks and identity proofing.
Disabling (not deleting) an account and resetting its password when someone leaves, so data can still be accessed later.
Setting an end date so temporary staff or contractor accounts disable automatically.
Administrators use a normal account for email and a separate privileged account for admin tasks.
AD stores X.500 objects addressed by distinguished names: DC (domain component), OU (organizational unit), CN (common name), e.g. CN=Computer1,OU=Sales,DC=DomainA,DC=com.
Security Identifier: unique ID assigned to every AD account.
Ticket Granting Ticket: Kerberos ticket issued at login (10-hour lifetime) used to request service tickets.
User exchanges a service ticket with a resource, which returns a session ticket; both sides verify each other. Provides SSO.
Clocks must be within 5 minutes of the domain controller or authentication fails; keep in sync with NTP.
Legacy Windows authentication using MD4 hashes; vulnerable to pass-the-hash. Replaced by Kerberos.
The Active Directory database file holding encrypted credentials.
/etc/passwd holds account info; /etc/shadow holds password hashes (root only). Create users with useradd and passwd.
Permissions assigned to groups (e.g. Sales, IT) rather than individuals; users inherit them by membership.
Access decisions that also consider location, time, device, network, and behavior.
Login from an unusual device or context that triggers extra verification (e.g. Dropbox emailing you about a new phone).
Verifying a person is who they claim (passport, driver's license, SSN) before issuing credentials.
Trust between organizations so one's users can be authenticated by their home identity provider to use another's services.
IdP issues and validates credentials; SP provides the resource and trusts the IdP's assertion.
XML-based standard for exchanging authentication/authorization assertions between an IdP and SP; used for federation and web SSO.
Open standard for delegated AUTHORIZATION using tokens, letting apps access resources without the user's password.
Authentication layer on top of OAuth; "Sign in with Google" to a third-party site.
One login gives access to many systems (Kerberos, SAML, OIDC); a compromised credential exposes everything.
Open-source federation (SAML) software; RADIUS federation is federation over wireless (e.g. eduroam).
Different identity systems working together, e.g. web apps using OAuth can't use Kerberos.
Confirming an entity's attributes or credentials through a trusted source: certificates, tokens, federation, AD.
Access by classification labels and clearance levels set by the system/owner; users can't change them. Used by the military.
Creates data and sets its classification; accountable for it.
Keeps data accurate and consistent; defines data quality and governance rules.
Technical role that stores, encrypts, backs up, and secures the data.
Access granted by job role (e.g. only two finance staff can sign checks).
Access determined by rules applied to everyone, e.g. firewall ACLs or time-of-day rules.
Fine-grained access based on attributes such as department, location, clearance, time, device.
The data owner decides who gets access, using ACLs (e.g. file permissions set by the file's creator).
Access only permitted during defined hours.
False acceptance rate: biometric system lets in an unauthorized person. The more dangerous error.
False rejection rate: biometric system rejects a legitimate user.
Crossover error rate: point where FAR equals FRR; lower CER = better biometric system.
Retina scans blood vessels at the back of the eye (needs precise light); iris scans the colored ring (used in biometric passports).
Biometric authentication by how a person walks.
Physical devices whose secrets never leave them: smart cards, fobs, security keys (YubiKey), SSH keys.
Software-based: passwords, PINs, OTPs, authenticator apps, knowledge-based questions.
One-time password valid for a short time (exam may say 30-60 seconds).
TOTP = time-based one-time password (expires after a time window). HOTP = HMAC/counter-based OTP that's valid until used.
Security questions or facts only the user should know (e.g. recent bank transactions).
Know = password, PIN. Have = smart card, token, phone. Are = biometrics.

cards.term: Something you do / somewhere you are
cards.def: Do = behavior such as gait, keystroke dynamics, signature. Somewhere = location (geolocation, IP).
Password + PIN = single factor (both "know"). Factors must come from different categories to count as 2FA/MFA.
Characters from at least three of four groups: lowercase, uppercase, numbers, special characters.
Favor long passphrases over short complex passwords.
Prevents reusing previous passwords.
Stops users changing their password repeatedly to cycle back to an old one.
Forces a password change after a set period.
Number of failed attempts before an account locks (often 3 or 5); defeats brute force.
Vault that generates and stores unique passwords behind a master password.
Login with biometrics, security keys, smart cards, or SSH keys instead of passwords (e.g. Face ID, FIDO2 passkeys).
Controls, monitors, and time-limits use of admin, service, and root accounts.
Privileges granted only when requested and approved, for a limited time, then revoked automatically.
Privileged account passwords stored in a vault and checked out only when approved; sessions often recorded.
Short-lived, single-use credentials valid only for the task's duration.
Separate hardened AD forest holding admin accounts, trusted by the production domain via a PAM trust.
Orchestration (integrating tools and APIs into workflows), automation (doing routine tasks), response (playbook actions like isolating hosts or blocking IPs).
Mean time to detect: average time to discover an incident; SOAR and automation reduce it.
Automated policies that keep systems within approved configurations so mistakes can't create vulnerabilities.
Automatically created and managed groups/rules controlling who or what can reach a resource (e.g. cloud security groups).
Automatically allocating and releasing VMs, storage, and network resources as needed.
Automation opens, prioritizes, assigns, and escalates tickets (e.g. ServiceDesk Plus) so critical incidents reach the right people fast.
Developers frequently merge code into a shared repository where it's automatically built and tested.
Automated tests run on code changes to confirm quality and that no vulnerabilities were introduced.
Connecting tools and systems through APIs so automation can move data and trigger actions across them.
Time saving, enforcing baselines, standard configurations, secure scaling, employee retention, faster reaction time, workforce multiplier.
Automation lets a small team do the work of a larger one by handling repetitive tasks.
Future cost and risk created by quick-fix shortcuts that will need rework later.
Relying on one automation system for critical functions; needs redundancy and failover.
Automation needs continuous maintenance and updates or it becomes outdated and vulnerable.
Preparation -> Detection -> Analysis -> Containment -> Eradication -> Recovery -> Lessons learned.
Build the IR plan, assemble the CSIRT, set up a discreet communication plan, document configurations, diagrams, and critical assets.
Cybersecurity Incident Response Team: the group trained and assigned to handle incidents.
Spotting abnormal behavior with EDR, IDS, syslog collectors, and SIEM.
Correlating and prioritizing the incident's type and impact, often using MITRE ATT&CK, Cyber Kill Chain, or the Diamond Model.
Limiting the damage: isolate/quarantine systems, collect volatile evidence, disable compromised accounts.
Removing the root cause: delete malware, patch, harden, disable unneeded services.
Restoring clean systems and data and returning to normal operations.
Post-incident review of what went well and what didn't, to improve the plan.
Public knowledge base of adversary groups (e.g. APT28), tactics, techniques, and mitigations.
Lockheed Martin model: reconnaissance, weaponization, delivery, exploitation, installation, command and control, actions on objectives.
Links four elements of an intrusion: adversary, capabilities, infrastructure, victim.
Red team attacks, blue team defends, white team oversees and judges the exercise.
Digging into WHY an incident happened so it can't recur (vs. lessons learned, which reviews the response).
Proactively searching for hidden attackers using an attacker's mindset, threat feeds, advisories, and intelligence fusion.
Combining many intelligence sources (OSINT, feeds, expert analysis) into one picture.
Collection -> Examination -> Analysis -> Reporting.
Order to preserve relevant data (e.g. a mailbox can't delete anything) during litigation or investigation, often without alerting the subject.
Documented record of everyone who handled evidence, with dates, times, and locations, proving it wasn't tampered with.
Record each device's time zone, then convert all evidence to one time zone (e.g. GMT) to build an accurate timeline.
Hash data before and after examination to prove it wasn't changed.
Collect the most volatile evidence first: CPU cache -> RAM -> swap/page file -> hard drive.
Gathering and searching electronic data (email, documents, databases) for legal proceedings.
Contract clause letting a customer audit a supplier's security and compliance.
Records allowed/blocked traffic with source and destination IP, port, protocol, and time; shows unauthorized access attempts.
Events, errors, and user interactions inside an application; context for app-specific incidents.
User activity, system changes, and security events on computers and phones.
Application, Security (failed logins, access changes), System (drivers, hardware), and Setup (installs/upgrades) logs.
Security events recorded by Windows, macOS, or Linux about OS health and access.
Record of detected or blocked attacks and suspicious traffic patterns.
Records connections, data transfers, and errors across the network; helps find breaches and data leaks.
Data about data: file timestamps (created, modified, accessed), authors, and photo GPS location; reveals who/what/when/where.
Records every domain looked up and failed resolutions; shows if a user visited malicious sites.
Records visitors' source IPs, HTTP status codes, and pages requested.
Scheduled reports that turn security data into real-time insight and compliance evidence.
Real-time visual display of key metrics and KPIs; makes security status understandable for non-technical managers.
Saved copy of network packets for deep analysis and forensics; captured with Wireshark or tcpdump.
Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge (DORA); seeing only the first packet in a capture points to a DHCP server problem.
Record of normal traffic patterns used to spot abnormal or malicious traffic.
Guidelines = flexible, recommended best practices. Policies = mandatory rules that must be followed.
Rules for how employees may use company resources: email, internet, social media.
Top-level policy defining how sensitive information is protected (access control, encryption, passwords).
Plan to keep essential business functions running during and after a disruption.
IT-focused plan for restoring systems and data after a disaster; narrower than the BCP.
Defines how security incidents are identified, reported, and handled.
Rules for securely developing, testing, and deploying software.
Waterfall = linear, each stage finishes before the next. Agile = short iterative sprints, faster delivery.
Development -> Test (regression testing) -> Staging (real data in a sandbox, QA, vulnerability scan) -> Production.
International standard for an Information Security Management System (ISMS); risk-based, continuous improvement, certifiable.
Catalog of security controls and best-practice guidance supporting ISO 27001.
Privacy extension to ISO 27001: Privacy Information Management System (PIMS); aligns with GDPR and CCPA.
Information security controls for cloud services, covering provider and customer shared responsibilities.
Protection of PII in public clouds (privacy in the cloud).
Catalog of security and privacy controls for US federal systems, widely adopted elsewhere.
Federal Information Processing Standards: NIST standards for US government systems (e.g. FIPS 140 for crypto modules).

cards.term: Privacy standards and laws to remember
cards.def: GDPR, CCPA, ISO 27701, ISO/IEC 27018.
Cloud access control that uses signals (user, device, location, risk) and conditions to allow, block, or require MFA.
Rotating gate letting one person through at a time.
RFID badge tapped on a reader for physical access.
Bringing in new staff: orientation, training, provisioning equipment and accounts, signing an NDA.
Exit process: return equipment, revoke access, exit interview.
Non-disclosure agreement: legal promise to keep company information confidential.
Detailed procedure guide for a specific scenario (incident type, disaster recovery).
Regulatory, legal, industry, local/regional (e.g. CCPA), national (e.g. HIPAA), global (e.g. PCI DSS).
Boards (strategic direction), committees (audit, compensation, security), government entities, centralized vs. decentralized.
Decides why and how personal data is processed; writes the policies and is legally accountable (e.g. for consent and privacy notices).
Processes data on the controller's behalf following its instructions; keeps an audit trail.
Senior person accountable for protecting a data set and enforcing its usage policy.
Stores, encrypts, backs up the data and applies retention and archiving.
Maintains data quality, metadata, and classification; works with custodians on controls.
Probability that an event causes financial loss or loss of service.
Someone or something that wants to cause loss by exploiting a vulnerability.
A weakness an attacker can exploit (unpatched software, misconfigured firewall).
First stage of risk management: identify and classify assets and the risks to them.
Unscheduled assessment triggered by a specific event or newly perceived threat.
Assessment scheduled at regular, predetermined intervals.
Assessment for a single project, system rollout, or organizational change.
Real-time, often automated, ongoing monitoring and analysis of risk.
Subjective ratings (high/medium/low) of likelihood and impact, often shown on a risk matrix/heat map.
Assigns numbers (dollars, frequencies) to risk: SLE, ARO, ALE.
Grid of likelihood vs. impact, colored by severity; a qualitative tool for presenting to management.
Single Loss Expectancy: cost of one occurrence. SLE = Asset Value x Exposure Factor.
Annualized Rate of Occurrence: how many times per year the event is expected (6 laptops lost/year = 6; once every 4 years = 0.25).
Annualized Loss Expectancy = SLE x ARO; expected loss per year, used to justify the cost of a control or insurance.
Percentage of an asset's value lost in one event (fire destroys 40% of the building = 0.4).
Numerical chance an event occurs, expressed from 0 to 1 (or 0-100%).
Qualitative expression of probability (high/medium/low).
Consequence of a risk event, often measured in money.
Log of identified risks with owners, KRIs, thresholds, severity, and planned responses.
Metric giving early warning that risk exposure is rising (e.g. spike in failed transactions).
Person or team accountable for managing a specific risk and its mitigation.
Level at which a risk becomes unacceptable and requires action.
Acceptable deviation around the risk appetite; the point at which the organization pulls back.
Amount of risk an organization is willing to take on in pursuit of its objectives.
Embraces higher risk for growth and innovation.
Prioritizes security and avoids risky opportunities.
Balanced; evaluates each risk case by case.
Shift the financial impact to a third party: insurance (incl. cyber insurance) or outsourcing.
Acknowledge the risk and deliberately take no action because the risk or cost to fix is low.
Formal, documented release from a policy requirement for a set period, often needing approval.
Approved, usually temporary deviation from a policy/standard, typically with compensating controls.
Stop or never start the risky activity.
Apply controls to reduce likelihood or impact (antivirus, patching, firewalls).
Raw risk before any controls are applied.
Risk remaining after controls are applied.
Communicating risk status to decision-makers and stakeholders; supports decisions, confidence, and compliance.
Identifies critical functions, single points of failure, and the operational and financial impact of a disruption; sets RTO and RPO.
Recovery Point Objective: maximum acceptable data loss measured in time; drives backup frequency (RPO 3 h = back up at least every 3 h).
Recovery Time Objective: maximum acceptable time to restore operations after a disruption.
Mean Time To Repair: average time to fix a failed component.
Mean Time Between Failures: average operating time between failures; higher = more reliable.
Background check of a supplier's security, competence, and reliability before and during a relationship.
Authorized, intrusive simulated attack on a vendor's systems to find exploitable weaknesses.
Pen test with no prior information (formerly black box); emulates an outside attacker.
Pen test with limited internal information (formerly gray box).
Pen test with full details including source code (formerly white box); most thorough.
Program paying outside researchers for vulnerabilities they find, scaled by severity.
Contract clause letting the customer audit the vendor's systems and processes, often at short notice.
Vendor's own audit reports, reviewed to judge its internal controls.
Unbiased third-party audit of a vendor (e.g. SOC 2 report, ISO certification audit).
Evaluating risk in the vendor's own suppliers and subcontractors (fourth parties).
Investigating a vendor's finances, operations, compliance, and track record before selecting it.
Relationship between a decision-maker and a vendor that could bias selection; must be disclosed and managed.
Service-Level Agreement: measurable service levels (uptime, response/resolution times) with penalties if missed.
Memorandum of Agreement: legally binding document of roles, responsibilities, and terms of cooperation.
Memorandum of Understanding: statement of intent and mutual goals; generally NOT legally binding.
Master Service Agreement: general terms for an ongoing relationship (payment, IP, liability, dispute resolution).
Statement of Work: specifics of one project under the MSA: tasks, deliverables, timelines, price.
Legally binding promise not to disclose confidential or proprietary information.
Business Partnership Agreement: contributions, decision-making, profit sharing, and termination terms for a joint venture.
Ongoing oversight of vendor performance and compliance against the contract.
Structured survey sent to vendors about security controls, compliance, finances (e.g. SIG, CAIQ).
Agreed expectations, responsibilities, communication protocols, and boundaries for working with a vendor or tester.
Self-assessment of adherence to the organization's own policies: policy adherence, regular audits, IR evaluation, risk assessment, training effectiveness.
Demonstrating adherence to outside regulations and standards (GDPR, HIPAA, PCI DSS) to regulators, auditors, clients, and partners.
Fines, sanctions, reputational damage, loss of license, contractual impacts.
Up to EUR 10 million or 2% of global annual turnover, whichever is higher.
Up to EUR 20 million or 4% of global annual turnover, whichever is higher.
Legal or regulatory penalties or restrictions imposed for non-compliance.
Regulator revokes the license to operate (banks, healthcare providers) after non-compliance.
Breach of contract, lawsuits, or terminated agreements resulting from non-compliance.
Investigating and understanding risks and obligations (the research/assessment part).
Acting on that knowledge: implementing and maintaining reasonable controls (doing the right thing).
Formal statement (often signed) confirming compliance or that a policy was read and will be followed.
Recording that a person received and understood a policy (e.g. signing the AUP).
Tools that continuously check configurations and controls and generate compliance reports.
Controller must notify the supervisory authority within 72 hours of becoming aware of a breach (Article 33).
Affected individuals must be notified without unreasonable delay and no later than 60 days after discovery.
The person whom personal data is about; holds rights such as access and erasure under GDPR.
Catalog of what data the organization holds, where it lives, its type, and how it is used.
Policy for how long each type of data must be kept, often set by regulation, then securely disposed of.
GDPR Article 17: a data subject can ask the controller to erase their personal data unless a legal reason requires keeping it.
EU regulation protecting personal data of people in the EU; applies to any organization worldwide processing their data.
California Consumer Privacy Act: state (local/regional) privacy law giving Californians control over their personal data.
US national law protecting health information (PHI).
Independent party examines and formally vouches for the accuracy or compliance of information (e.g. SOC 2 report).
Audit run by the organization's own auditors: compliance, audit committee oversight, self-assessments.
Checks that activities follow applicable rules and regulations; reported to senior management and the audit committee.
Board-level committee overseeing the internal audit function; reports to the board of directors.
Internal stakeholders evaluate their own processes to find weaknesses and improve; results used internally.
Audit by an independent outside firm: regulatory, examinations, assessments, independent third-party audits.
External check that the organization follows the regulations of its industry; reported to regulators.
Detailed review of financial records against GAAP or IFRS for accuracy and completeness.
External evaluation of internal controls, risk management, and governance with improvement recommendations.
Impartial auditor's opinion on statements, operations, and controls; builds trust with outsiders.
Testing physical security: tailgating, lock picking, badge cloning, breaking into the server room.
Simulated attack by ethical hackers to find weaknesses; red team.
Tests the organization's ability to detect and respond to attacks; blue team.
Combines physical and digital (and offensive/defensive) testing for a holistic view.
Tester gets full information about systems (formerly white box).
Tester gets limited information (formerly gray box).
Tester gets no prior information (formerly black box).
Gathering information without touching the target's systems: OSINT, WHOIS, search engines, social media, public DNS records.
Directly interacting with target systems: port scans (Nmap), vulnerability scans (Nessus, OpenVAS), fingerprinting; can be detected.
Network mapper: discovers hosts, open ports, running services, and OS versions (active recon).
Open-source intelligence: publicly available information about a target.
Untargeted fraudulent email sent widely to trick people into giving up credentials, money, or clicking malware.
Targeted phishing aimed at a specific person or group, using details about them.
Phishing aimed at executives (CEO, CFO).
Phishing via SMS text messages.
Voice phishing over the phone.
IT sends simulated phishing emails to staff; those who click get remedial training. Measures and improves resistance.
Spoofed sender or look-alike domain, urgent/threatening language, prize or tax-refund lures, requests for personal info, mismatched links, Reply-To differs from From.
Hovering over a link shows its real destination URL before clicking.
Don't click links or open attachments, report it to IT/security, change passwords if credentials may be exposed.
Spotting unusual patterns in users or systems: risky, unexpected, or unintentional behavior.
Not necessarily malicious but dangerous: sharing credentials, excessive permissions, ignoring warnings, downloading suspicious files.
Deviation from normal patterns: a user suddenly accessing sensitive data, logins at odd hours, unusual resource use.
Human error: misconfiguration, accidental data leak, being tricked by social engineering.
SOPs, AUP, and security policies communicated to staff and regularly reviewed.
Staying alert to threats around you and understanding the consequences of your actions (shoulder surfing, tailgating, odd requests).
Teach staff to recognize and report malicious insiders and unwitting accomplices.
Strong, unique passwords, password managers, and MFA.
USB drives and cables (e.g. O.MG cable) can carry malware; never plug in unknown devices; scan media.
Securing day-to-day activities: careful communication, encryption, handling suspicious events, reporting incidents.
Secure remote access, VPN use, home Wi-Fi security, risks of personal devices, public Wi-Fi.
Goals/needs -> develop -> deliver -> feedback -> monitor -> back to goals.
Measure training impact soon after rollout (e.g. drop in phishing click rate or account compromises).
Re-measure over time (e.g. 6 months later); retrain if incidents rise from complacency.
Quizzes, challenges, leaderboards to make training engaging and improve retention.
Exercises that mimic real attacks so staff practice spotting and responding.
